div.p: The race of the Caesars became extinct with Nero. That this would happen was made manifest by a multitude of portents, and especially by two of unmistakable clearness. Many years before, when Livia immediately after her marriage to Augustus was revisiting her estate at Veii, an eagle which flew past dropped in her lap a white hen, holding in its beak a sprig of laurel, as when the eagle had carried it off. She thought it good to have the fowl tended and the sprig planted, and such a brood of chickens was produced, that to this day that villa is called "The Villa of the Hens," and such a grove of laurel-trees, that the Caesars plucked from it their laurels when going to celebrate a triumph; also it became an established custom for those who triumphed to plant at once those laurel branches in the same place, and it was observed that at the death of a Caesar the tree planted by him withered away. So in Nero's last year the whole grove shrivelled from the roots up, and all the hens that were there died. Moreover, when shortly afterwards the temple of the Caesars was struck by lightning, the heads fell from all the statues at once, and even the sceptre of Augustus was dashed from his hands.

Nero was succeeded by Galba, who was connected in no degree with the house of the Caesars, though undoubtedly most nobly born and of a great and ancient family, seeing that in the inscriptions on his statues he always added that he was a great-grandson of Quintus Catulus Capitolinus, and as emperor he displayed in the hall of the palace a family-tree in which he traced back his father's line to Jupiter, and his mother's to Pasiphaë, wife of Minos.

To recount the famous ancestors and the titles of this whole race would be a lengthy tale; I shall, therefore, briefly touch on those of his own particular family. It is a disputed point which of the Sulpicii first bore the surname of Galba, why he adopted it, and whence he derived it. Some think that it was because after having for a long time and to no purpose besieged a town in Spain he set fire to it at last by torches smeared with galbanum; others, because during a protracted illness he made constant use of galbeum, that is to say, remedies wrapped in wool; others, again, because he was very fat in form, such a one as the Gauls call galba, or, on the contrary, because he was as slender as the insects named galbae, which are bred in oak-trees.

Much lustre was added to the family by Servius Galba, who held the office of consul, and was quite the greatest orator of his day. It was he who, as history tells, while governing Spain as propraetor, caused the war with Viriathus by treacherously massacring thirty thousand Lusitanians. His grandson, being incensed against Julius Caesar (to whom he had been a lieutenant in Gaul) by reason of his defeat for the consulship, joined in the conspiracy with Cassius and Brutus, and was consequently condemned to banishment under the Pedian law.

From him were descended the grandfather and father of the emperor Galba. The grandfather, who was more famous for his literary pursuits than for his political honours, for he did not rise above the rank of praetor, published a very comprehensive history, which showed considerable care. The father held the consulship, and although he was undersized and hunchbacked as well, and had but moderate ability as a speaker, was a diligent pleader in the courts.

He was married to Mummia Achaica, granddaughter of Catulus and great-granddaughter of Lucius Mummius, who destroyed Corinth; and after her to Livia Ocellina, a lady of very great wealth and beauty, though it is thought that it was she who set herself to win him on account of his high descent, and all the more eagerly when he, after repeated advances on her part, removed his robe in private and revealed his disfigurement, lest he should be thought to be imposing on her ignorance. By Achaica he was the father of two sons, Gaius and Servius, of whom the elder, Gaius, left Rome after draining his resources, and when he was debarred by Tiberius from the drawing of lots for proconsulships in his proper year, he put an end to his own life.

The emperor Servius Galba was born in the consulship of Marcus Valerius Messala and Gnaeus Lentulus, on the ninth day before the Kalends of January, in a country-house standing on a hill near Terracina, on the left as one goes to Fundi. Being adopted by his stepmother, he took the name Livius and the surname Ocella, and also changed his forename, for afterwards he used that of Lucius instead of Servius till he came to be emperor. It is well known that once when he came with other boys of his own age to pay his respects to Augustus, the emperor pinched his little cheek and said: "Thou too, my child, wilt nibble at this imperial power of mine." Tiberius also, on being informed that Galba would one day be emperor, but not before old age, remarked: "Let him live, then, since that does not concern me."

Moreover, as his grandfather was sacrificing to avert the evil boded by a lightning-bolt, and an eagle snatched the entrails from his hands and bore them to an acorn-yielding oak, the soothsayer when consulted made reply that imperial dignity would come unto the house, but not till late; whereupon he scoffingly observed: "Aye, when a mule has a foal!" Afterwards, when Galba was venturing on his revolt, nothing gave him such confidence as the foaling of a mule, and while others were shocked at this as an ill-omened portent, he alone regarded it as most auspicious, calling to mind the sacrifice and the utterance of his grandfather.

When he had donned the robe of manhood, he dreamt that the goddess Fortune said to him that she was weary of standing before his door, and that, unless she were admitted speedily, she would be a prey to the first comer. On waking, he opened the door of the entrance-hall, and found near the threshold a bronze statue of the goddess, more than a cubit in height; this he carried in his bosom to Tusculum, where he usually passed the summer, consecrated it in an apartment of his house, and worshipped it from that time on with monthly devotions and a yearly all-night vigil.

Even when he was not yet of mature years, he kept up most persistently an ancient and obsolete Roman usage, which lingered only in his household, that the freedmen and slaves should present themselves in a body before him twice a day, and that in the morning one by one they should bid him “Good morrow," and at eventime "Good night."

Among other liberal studies he applied himself to law. He also dutifully married, but after the loss of his wife Lepida and the two sons whom he had by her, he continued a widower, and could not be tempted by any match, not even with Agrippina, who had been widowed by the death of Domitius, and who, while Galba was still a married man and not yet a widower, tried to attract him by every artifice, so much so that at a gathering of matrons she was sharply rebuked and even slapped by the mother of Lepida.

He showed especial respect to Livia Augusta, by whose favour during her lifetime he enjoyed very great influence, and by whose will at her death he came near to being enriched. She left him a legacy of fifty million sesterces in priority to the other legacies; but since this sum was only marked in figures and not written fully in words, Tiberius, who was her heir, reduced it to five hundred thousand sesterces, and even this amount Galba did not receive.

He entered on political office before the legal time, and during his praetorship, at the celebration of the games in honour of Flora, he exhibited a novel kind of spectacle, rope-walking elephants. Then he governed the province of Aquitania for about a year; next he held for six months an ordinary consulship, in which, as it so chanced, he succeeded Lucius Domitius, the father of Nero, and was himself succeeded by Salvius Otho, father of the emperor, which was like a presage of what happened later, when he became emperor in the period between their two sons.

Being appointed by Gaius Caesar in the room of Gaetulicus, on the day after his arrival among the legions, when he noticed them applauding at one of the stated festivals which chanced to fall at that time, he checked them by issuing an Order of the Day that they were to keep their hands within their cloaks. At once this line passed from mouth to mouth throughout the camp: "Soldier, learn to soldier; Galba, not Gaetulicus, is here!"

With equal rigour he forbade requests for furlough. Veterans and recruits alike he hardened by continual work. Moreover, he put a speedy check on the barbarians, whose inroads had extended to the very borders of Gaul, and he so commended himself and his army to the approval of Gaius, then present in person, that of the countless forces brought together from all the provinces there were none who received greater praise or greater rewards. He himself earned special distinction when, after directing, shield in hand, the field manœuvres, he actually ran for twenty miles by the side of the emperor's chariot.

On the news of the murder of Gaius, though many urged him to seize the opportunity, he preferred quietude. By this he won very great favour with Claudius, who admitted him to his suite of friends and had so high an opinion of his worth that he postponed the date of the expedition to Britain because Galba was attacked by a sudden disorder of no great seriousness. For two years he administered Africa as proconsul, being selected without lot to restore order in that province, which was disturbed by internal feuds and a rising of the barbarians. This he did by the very careful observance of strict discipline and justice even in the most trivial matters.

When a soldier, on an expedition where supplies were very tight, was charged with selling for a hundred denarii a peck of corn which remained over from his rations, he gave orders that when this soldier began to be in want of food he should receive help from no one, and so he wasted to death through hunger. Again, when he was dispensing justice, a case came before him of the ownership of a sumpter-mule, and as the proofs and witnesses on either side were unconvincing, and so it was difficult to divine the truth, he decided that the animal should be led with muffled head to its usual drinking-pool, that then its head should be uncovered, and it should become the property of him to whom it returned of its own accord after being watered.

As a reward for his achievements, both at that time in Africa and earlier in Germany, he received the insignia of a triumph, and a triple priesthood, being admitted a member of the college of Fifteen, the confraternity of Titius, and the college of the priests of Augustus. From that time to near the middle of Nero's reign he lived almost wholly in retirement, never even starting on a drive for health's sake without having close at hand a carriage conveying a million sesterces in gold; until finally, when he was staying at the town of Fundi, the province of Hispania Tarraconensis was offered to him.

And it happened that after his entry into this province, as he was sacrificing in a public temple, the hair of the young acolyte who bore the censer suddenly turned white all over his head, and there were not wanting interpreters to declare that this meant a change of rulers, and that an old man should succeed a young; that is to say, that Galba should succeed Nero. Not long afterwards a thunderbolt fell into a lake in Cantabria, and in this lake were found twelve axes, an unmistakable sign of imperial power.

For eight years he governed the province in a variable and uneven manner. At first he was keen, vigorous, and in punishing misdeeds even harsh beyond measure. For in the case of a money-changer who was fraudulent in his dealings, he cut off his hands and nailed them to his counting-table; a guardian who had poisoned his ward, whose inheritance he was to get in case of death, he sentenced to crucifixion, and when the condemned invoked the benefit of the laws and protested that he was a Roman citizen, Galba, making a pretence of lightening his punishment by the consolation of some special distinction, ordered his cross to be changed and one much higher than the rest and painted white to be set up for him. But little by little he changed to inactivity and sloth, that he might not give Nero any handle, and, as he used to say himself, because no one could be compelled to render an account of his idle time.

He was holding the assizes at New Carthage when he learned of the rising in the Gallic provinces through an entreaty for help from the governor of Aquitania; this was followed by a letter from Vindex urging him to lend himself as the liberator and leader of mankind. Without long deliberation, he accepted this proposal, partly through fear, partly through hope. For he had surprised despatches directing his own death, which had been secretly sent by Nero to his agents. At the same time his confidence was being strengthened not merely by the most favourable auspices and omens but also by the prediction of a noble maiden, and the more so because the priest of Jupiter at Clunia, prompted by a dream, had brought to light from the inmost shrine of the temple these very same prophetic lines, delivered in like fashion by a soothsaying maid two hundred years before. The burden of these lines was that one day there should come forth from Spain a prince and master of the world.

Accordingly, under the pretence that he was going to deal with cases of manumission, he mounted the tribunal, on which in front of him was placed every procurable bust of those condemned and executed by Nero; and having by his side a boy of noble birth, whom he had fetched for this very purpose from his place of exile in the nearest of the Balearic isles, he deplored the condition of the times, and when he was hailed by all as emperor, he professed himself to be merely the legate of the senate and people of Rome.

Then he announced a cessation of public business, and enrolled from the lower classes in the province legions and auxiliaries to supplement his old army of one legion, two squadrons, and three cohorts; while out of the nobles who were eminent for their wisdom and their years he established a sort of senate, to which more important matters could be referred when occasion arose.

Further, he chose from the equestrian order young men, who, retaining their right to rings of gold, should have the title of volunteers, and should keep guard by watches about his bedchamber instead of legionary soldiers. He also sent proclamations throughout the provinces, calling on all individually and collectively to join the movement and to aid the common cause in whatever way they severally could.

Much about the same time, during the fortification of a town which he had chosen as a base of operations, a ring was found of antique workmanship, the carving on the gem depicting a Victory with a trophy; and straightway there reached the quay at Dertosa an Alexandrian vessel laden with arms, without a pilot, without a sailor, without a passenger, so that none felt any doubt that the war which was being undertaken was just and holy and blessed by heaven. Then suddenly and unexpectedly the whole plan came near to being upset.

One of the two cavalry squadrons, repenting of its change of allegiance, attempted to desert Galba as he approached the camp, and was with difficulty kept loyal to him; and certain slaves, who had been primed for treachery and presented to him by one of Nero's freedmen, well-nigh succeeded in slaying him as he was passing through an alley to the baths, had it not been that they were heard encouraging each other not to lose the opportunity, and being questioned as to what opportunity they meant, a confession was wrung from them by torture.

To these great perils was added the death of Vindex, by which above all else he was stricken with panic, and like one utterly forlorn came near abandoning life. But when messengers arrived from the city with the news that Nero was slain
and that all had sworn allegiance to him, he laid aside the title of legate and assumed that of Caesar. He entered on his march to Rome in a commander's cloak, with a dagger hanging from his neck in front of his breast; and he did not resume the wearing of the toga until he had crushed the plotters of sedition, Nymphidius Sabinus, prefect of the praetorian guards at Rome, in Germany Fonteius Capito, in Africa Clodius Macer, governors of provinces.

He was preceded by a reputation for cruelty and avarice combined; for it was said that he had punished the cities in the several provinces of Spain and Gaul which had been slow to join his cause by heavier tributes, and some even by the levelling of their walls, and that he had inflicted the penalty of death upon military officers and upon procurators, together with their wives and children; further, that he had melted down a golden crown of fifteen pounds in weight, presented by the people of Tarraco from their ancient temple of Jupiter, and had ordered the three ounces wanting in the weight to be exacted from them.

This reputation was confirmed and increased upon his first entrance into Rome. When he wished to compel the marines, whom Nero had turned from rowers into regular soldiers, to go back to their old position, and they refused and even claimed more stoutly an eagle and standards, he not merely dispersed them with a charge of cavalry, but also decimated them. Moreover, he disbanded a cohort of Germans, which had been organised by the early Caesars to act as a bodyguard, and had proved itself most faithful in many a trial, and sent them back to their country without a bounty, alleging that they were too favourably disposed to Gnaeus Dolabella, near whose gardens they were encamped.

These stories too, whether true or false, were circulated in ridicule of him: that when an unusually sumptuous banquet was served, he uttered a groan; that when his steward in ordinary presented his abstract of accounts, he handed him a dish of pulse as a reward for assiduity and exactness; and that when the flute-player Canus had given him wondrous pleasure, he presented him with five denarii, producing them with his own hand out of his private purse.

For these reasons his coming was not so very welcome, and this was made evident at the next theatrical show; for
when the actors in the Atellan burlesque began the well-known song, "Onesimus is back in town," with one accord the spectators rendered the rest of it in chorus, and went through it several times with fitting gestures, always starting from that line.

He enjoyed much greater popularity and respect when winning the empire than when ruling it, though he gave many proofs of being an excellent prince; but these did not command a favour commensurate with the odium excited by his acts of a different character.

He was under the arbitrary control of three men, who, as they lived along with him in the Palace and never left his side, were commonly known as his "pedagogues." These were Titus Vinius, an old lieutenant of his in Spain, a man of boundless greed; Cornelius Laco, a judge's adviser promoted to be prefect of the praetorian guards, who was intolerable alike through his arrogance and indolence; and his own freedman Icelus, who only a very short time before had been dignified by receiving the gold rings and the surname Marcianus, but was already a candidate for the highest post attainable by those of knight's estate. To the base purposes of these men, each a villain in a separate department of vice, he yielded and surrendered himself so passively that it became difficult to reconcile his actions; for at one time he showed himself more rigorous and parsimonious, at another time more slack and careless than befitted an elected emperor and one of his time of life.

Some illustrious members of the senatorial and equestrian orders he condemned on the most shadowy suspicion, and without hearing their defence. He rarely granted Roman citizenship. while the privileges of such as had three children he granted reluctantly to but one or two, and even to them only for a fixed and definite period. When the jurymen petitioned to have a sixth panel added, he not merely refused, but even deprived them of the concession which they owed to Claudius of not being summoned to trials during the winter and the beginning of the year.

It was thought too that he proposed to limit the tenure of senatorial and equestrian offices to a period of two years, and to give them only to those who were reluctant to take them or who declined them. As for the bounties of Nero, he appointed a commission of fifty Roman knights to revoke and recover them, not leaving more than a tenth to the beneficiaries, with a requirement that even if actors or athletes had sold anything that had formerly been given them, it should be taken away from the purchasers, in cases where the original recipients had expended the purchase-money and were not able to refund it.

On the other hand, there was nothing which he did not allow his retinue and his freedmen to sell at a price or bestow as a favour: taxes, exemptions from taxes, the punishment of the innocent, the pardoning of the guilty. Nay, more, when the Roman people demanded the execution of Halotus and Tigillinus, it was just these two-quite the most mischievous of all the agents of Nero-whom he saved from danger, and, moreover, he honoured Halotus with a very high procuratorship, and in the interests of Tigillinus he issued an edict rebuking the people for their inhumanity.

By such conduct he gave offence to almost every class, and kindled a peculiarly intense hatred in the minds of the soldiers. For their commanders had promised an unusually large donative to those who swore allegiance to him in his absence, but he refused to ratify it, and repeatedly declared that it was his practice to levy soldiers, not to buy them, and on this account he exasperated all the troops, wherever stationed. Moreover, he roused the fears and indignation of the praetorians by removing many of their number from time to time as suspected persons and adherents of Nymphidius.

But above all others the army of Upper Germany kept grumbling at being robbed of the rewards of their services against the Gauls and against Vindex. Consequently they were the first to venture to break their allegiance by refusing on the Kalends of January to take the oath of fealty unless in the name of the senate; and they at once decided on the despatch of envoys to the praetorians with a message that the emperor created in Spain was not to their liking, and that the praetorians themselves should choose one who would win the approval of all the armies.

When Galba received tidings of this, he thought that it was not so much his age as his childlessness which excited contempt, and so of a sudden he took from the midst of the throng of morning callers Piso Frugi Licinianus, an exceptional young man, nobly born, whom he had highly esteemed for long and had always designated in his will as heir to his estate and name. Calling him his son, he led him to the camp, where he adopted him in presence of the assembled soldiers; but even then he made no mention of largess, thus affording Marcus Salvius Otho an easier opportunity of effecting his designs within six days after the adoption.

Striking prodigies following one upon another from the very beginning of his reign had portended for him such an end as actually was his. When victims were being slain on the right hand and the left at every town all along his route from Spain, a bull, maddened by the stroke of an axe, broke its rope, rushed upon his chariot, and raising up its fore-feet drenched him with its blood; and as he alighted, one of his bodyguard, pushed forward by the crowd, nearly wounded him with his lance. Also, as he entered the city and then the Palace, he was welcomed by an earthquake and a sound like the bellowing of oxen.

Next followed signs much more unmistakable. He had set aside from all the treasure a necklace strung with pearls and jewels, to adorn therewith his statue of Fortune at Tusculum: of a sudden, thinking that it was worthy of a more stately place, he dedicated it to Venus of the Capitol; and on the very next night he dreamt that Fortune appeared to him, complaining that she was being robbed of the gift intended for her, and threatening that she too would take back what she had given to him. And when the terrified Galba, thinking to avert the evil boded by the dream, had sent forward at dawn ministers to make ready a sacrifice, and then himself had posted out to Tusculum, he found there nothing but warm ashes on the altar and beside it an old man all in black, holding the incense in a dish of glass and the wine in an earthen cup.

It was also remarked that as he was sacrificing on the Kalends of January, the chaplet fell from his head; that as he took the auspices, the chickens flew away; that on the day of the adoption when he was about to address the soldiers, the camp-stool, usually placed at the front of the tribunal, had been forgotten by the servants; and that in the senate his curule chair had been set awry.

As he was sacrificing on the morning of his murder, the soothsayer gave him many a warning to be on his guard against danger, since assassins were not far away. A few hours afterwards he learned that the praetorian camp was in the possession of Otho, and when most of his friends urged him to go there without delay, assuring him that by his authority and presence he could get the upper hand, he decided to do nothing more than keep within the Palace and strengthen his defence by bringing in guards from the legionaries who were quartered in many different parts of the city. However, he put on a corslet of linen, though he did not disguise the fact that it would be of little use against so many sword-points.

But he was lured out by false reports which the conspirators had deliberately spread to entice him on to the streets, while some kept hastily asserting that the affair was settled, that the mutineers were crushed, and that all the rest were thronging to the Palace to congratulate him, ready to render him full obedience. He went forth to meet them so confidently that upon a soldier's boasting that he had slain Otho, his only answer was, "On whose authority?'' and he continued on his way as far as the Forum. There the horsemen who had been commissioned to despatch him, forcing their horses through the thoroughfares and scattering the crowd of civilians, caught sight of him at a distance and halted for a moment; then they renewed their gallop and cut him down, deserted by all his followers.

Some relate that at the first uproar he cried out: "What means your conduct, fellow-soldiers? I am yours, and you are mine," and that he even promised them a largess. But the general account is that he of himself offered his throat to them, urging them to do their work and strike the blow, since so they thought good. The most astonishing thing would seem to be that none of those present made any effort to aid their emperor, and that of those who were summoned to the rescue one and all ignored the message, except a detachment from Germany. They, on account of a recent kindness of his in treating them with every care when they were sick and feeble, flew to his help, but came too late, delayed by the roundabout route which they took through not knowing the parts of the city.

He was slain at the Lake of Curtius, and was left lying just as he was, until a common soldier, returning from receiving his allowance of corn, threw down his load and cut off the head, and since there was no hair for him to grasp it by, he hid it in the bosom of his robe; later he thrust his thumb into the mouth, and in this way carried it to Otho. He made a present of it to the sutlers and soldiers' servants, who fixed it on the point of a pike and bore it in derision around the camp, shouting from time to time: "Galba, thou Cupid, have joy of thy youth!" What specially provoked them to such ribaldry was the fact that a few days earlier a report had gone abroad that when he was complimented on the bloom and freshness of his person, he had replied: "Unshaken still my strength abides." A freedman of Patrobius Neronianus bought the head from them for a hundred gold pieces and threw it into the place where, by Galba's order, his patron had been executed. It was late when at last his steward Argivus buried it and the rest of the body in Galba's pleasure-gardens adjoining the Aurelian Way.

He was of normal stature, and had a very bald head, blue eyes, and a hooked nose. His hands and feet were so twisted with gout that he could not abide a shoe, or unroll a small scroll, or even hold it at all. Moreover, the flesh on his left side had grown out and hung down in such a mass that it could with difficulty be held up even by a bandage.

It is said that he was a huge eater, and that in winter he usually took food even before dawn, while at dinner he was so plentifully supplied that he used to order his leavings to be carried round in big handfuls and distributed among the slaves who stood in attendance on the diners. In his desires he was more inclined to those of his own sex, and such of them as were well hardened and past their prime. It was told of him that in Spain, when Icelus, one of his old favourites, arrived with tidings of Nero's death, he not merely welcomed him openly with the most passionate kisses, but begged him to be made smooth without delay, and took him aside.

He perished in the seventy-third year of his age and in the seventh month of his reign. The senate, when first it had a free hand, had decreed to him a statue to be erected on a beaked column in the part of the Forum where he had been butchered; but Vespasian annulled the decree, believing that Galba had secretly sent assassins from Spain to Judaea to murder him.
